title: Lucy Stone and Henry Blackwell's Marriage Protest
text:
Lucy Stone was one of the best known American speakers for the abolition of slavery and for women's rights. She had long said she would never marry, because the law at the time gave a husband control over his wife's property, earnings, children and even her person. Henry Blackwell, a businessman and abolitionist, courted her for two years and promised that their marriage would be a partnership of equals.

They married on 1 May 1855 at her family home in West Brookfield, Massachusetts. The minister, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, was a fellow reformer. Before the ceremony, Lucy and Henry read aloud a protest they had written together. While declaring their affection for each other, they protested against the laws that gave the husband custody of the wife's person, the exclusive control and guardianship of their children, and ownership of her property, and that made a married woman's legal existence disappear into her husband's. Henry renounced the rights the law gave him.

Higginson sent the protest to the newspapers, and it was widely reprinted. Lucy Stone also kept her own name after marriage, almost unheard of at the time. Women who later followed her example were called "Lucy Stoners."

The couple worked side by side for women's suffrage for the rest of their lives. In 1870 they founded the Woman's Journal, which their daughter, Alice Stone Blackwell, later edited.
lesson: A marriage can begin with a public promise of equality. Partners who name the unfair rules around them are better placed to live differently.
people: Lucy Stone, Henry Blackwell, Thomas Wentworth Higginson
source: Marriage of Lucy Stone under Protest (1855), published in the Worcester Spy and the Liberator; Andrea Moore Kerr, Lucy Stone (1992)
